title: Eastern Promises
full_review:
"Eastern Promises" (Focus) is a taut, grippingly powerful story of the Russian underworld in London, and of Anna, a midwife at a London hospital (Naomi Watts) -- living with her mother, Helen (Sinead Cusack), and her late Russian father's brother, Stepan (Jerzy Skolimowski) -- as she tries to locate the family of a Russian teenager, Tatiana, who died giving birth.

Anna -- who, having become pregnant out of wedlock in a prior relationship, has just lost a baby herself -- feels particularly empathetic, and when she finds the girl's diary (written in Russian, of course), she thinks it may contain clues to track down her family.

She turns to a local Trans-Siberian restaurant and its seemingly avuncular owner, Semyon (Armin Mueller-Stahl), who's actually a member of the "Vory V Zakone" criminal brotherhood.

He has an alcoholic, power-hungry son, Kirill (Vincent Cassel), and a taciturn chauffeur, Nikolai (Viggo Mortensen), who stoically takes Kirill's verbal abuse and patronizing bossiness.

Anna hands a copy of the diary to Semyon -- who'd much rather have the original -- but Uncle Stepan begins to translate the original himself, and soon realizes it contains dangerous material that could put them all in deep water if the contents were revealed.

Meanwhile, Semyon confirms what he suspected all along: It contains incriminating information about Kirill. He bullies his way into Anna's hospital and offers her a deal: the whereabouts of the girl's parents in return for the original diary, which Uncle Stepan urges her to surrender.

Nikolai is Semyon's chosen emissary. The family hands over the diary, but the promised address is not forthcoming. What can Anna do? To say more would reveal too much of a plot full of surprises.

Director David Cronenberg's somber thriller has an intelligent script by Steve Knight and the film is executed with much the same artistry he brought to 2005's equally provocative "A History of Violence."

As in "The Godfather" films, Cronenberg and Knight skillfully show us enough of the surface normalcy in the milieu of the restaurant, such as an extended family gathering, that the criminal elements underneath the surface are all the more chilling. The characters, too, are exceptionally well drawn, and well played. Mortensen follows up his earlier collaboration with Cronenberg with another indelible portrayal and sports a fine Slavic accent, too.

Viewers must be cautioned that although the violence here is artistically valid some of it is quite strong and not for the faint-hearted. Within the film's first few minutes, for instance, someone's throat is graphically slashed, leading one to fear that the film will be nothing but a bloodbath. But no. Though the scene does foreshadow more violence to come, including a brutal encounter in a public bathhouse, mainly it gives the viewer an ongoing feeling of dread as if anything might happen. There is also a graphic sexual encounter with a sex slave, which is arguably justified here in context.

Much like the similarly themed "Trade," which charts sex trafficking between Mexico and the United States, this film offers another horrifying perspective on that same problem, as the United Kingdom's operation is said to be run by criminals of Eastern European descent.

And for all its sordid elements, this is also a story of great heroism and sacrifice, with positive human values coming into play at key moments.

The film contains brutal violence with bloodshed, the mutilation of a corpse, a graphic sexual act, rear and fleeting full-frontal-male and upper-female nudity, blood hemorrhaging, an extended tattooing sequence, rough language and profanity, and drug and rape references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
